expectations.text: Acknowledges that node selection is a substantive theoretical choice, not a neutral one, and that network structure depends on which items are included
expectations.evidence: "Under the network approach, nodes are not neutral observables — they are theoretical commitments about what the meaningful psychological entities are. The network structure you estimate is entirely determined by which nodes you put in. Add a node, remove a node, split a node, and you get a different graph."

expectations.text: References Fried's work on node selection, depression symptom heterogeneity, or the 'What are good depression symptoms' / '52 symptoms' line of work — OR makes the equivalent substantive point without the citation
expectations.evidence: "This is what Fried and colleagues have been pressing since at least 2015–2016 (the '52 symptoms of major depression' paper; 'What are good depression symptoms?')."

expectations.text: Mentions node redundancy / topological overlap as a methodological concern (near-duplicate items inflate edge weights)
expectations.evidence: "Several Y-BOCS items...are conceptually adjacent enough that they may have nearly identical conditioning sets. When that happens, the graphical lasso produces a spuriously strong edge between them, and those nodes' centrality estimates get inflated by the redundancy rather than by genuine psychological importance."

expectations.text: Suggests checking for redundant nodes (e.g., networktools, goldbricker) or justifying selection theoretically
expectations.evidence: "Run `networktools::goldbricker()` before estimation:" — followed by explicit R code using goldbricker with specific parameters (p = 0.05, method = 'hittner2003', threshold = 0.25).
